transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you. Could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Nice to meet you, Dr. Smith. Well, I suppose what brought me in is... I just keep getting up. Like, in meetings or at dinner, when everyone else is seated and settled. I'll suddenly feel like I need to go refill my coffee, or walk to the back of the room to check a handout, even though nothing is really urgent at all. 

We have these incredibly long staff meetings at the school—I teach tenth-grade history, which I usually love because the kids are finally old enough to understand real historical nuance, you know? Though this year the administration changed our textbooks and it has been an absolute headache trying to adapt my lesson plans. I spent practically all weekend just redoing my unit on the Industrial Revolution. 

But anyway, yes, I'll just stand up in the middle of all that. Or even at home during dinner. My husband made this wonderful pot roast on Sunday—he’s been watching that new British cooking show and trying out all the recipes, which is nice for me because I don't have to cook as much—and I just kept popping up from the table for no real reason...
Have you always felt this need to keep moving, or is this something that has only started more recently?

Well, I suppose I've always been a bit of a doer, but... it's definitely gotten noticeably harder to manage recently. I'd say for about eight months now? Yes, right around eight months, because that’s when my youngest left for college. 

She went all the way out to Oregon, which was quite a trek for us to get her moved in. We had to rent one of those massive moving vans, and let me tell you, my husband driving that thing through the mountain passes was absolutely terrifying. I kept telling him to pull over and let me drive, or at least slow down, but he is so stubborn when he gets behind the wheel of a large vehicle. We ended up having to stop at this quirky little motel in Northern California because it started pouring rain. 

But anyway, since she moved out, the house has just become so much quieter. It used to be constantly full of teenagers and cello practice—she’s first chair, actually, she's been playing since she was six—and now it's just me and my husband. And I think without all that noise and chaos, the quiet just sort of... echoes? I don't know, but since the house got so quiet, I just can't seem to stay sitting down.
When you feel this urge to stand up and move around, does it feel like you are doing it to relieve an internal sense of jitteriness or physical restlessness inside your body?

Yes, exactly, it's like this sort of... buzzing or jittery energy. If I can't actually get up and walk around, like when I'm sitting at my desk grading essays or when we're in church, I just end up shifting around in my seat so much. I'll catch myself tapping my foot, or clicking my pen over and over, and I really have to mentally remind myself to just settle down. 

Which is terribly difficult during church lately, to be honest, because Reverend Davis has been doing this incredibly long sermon series on the minor prophets. And, well, he’s a lovely man, he really is, but his delivery is just so monotone. His wife, on the other hand, is an absolute delight. She brought this amazing lemon pound cake to the choir fundraiser last week. I used to bake a lot of pound cakes when the girls were little, but you really need a heavy cast-aluminum bundt pan for it to bake evenly, and my favorite one got all scratched up years ago when my husband tried to wash it with steel wool. I told him you can't use abrasive sponges on non-stick coating, but he never checks the labels on the cleaning supplies...

Beyond the restlessness you've described, do you find that you spend a significant amount of your day worrying about various things—like your job, your family's health, or your finances—to the point where it feels difficult to control those thoughts?

Worrying? No, not really. I mean, I care about my family, of course, and I want my students to do well, but I wouldn't say I'm overwhelmed by worry or anything like that. I don't sit around agonizing over the bills or whatever. My husband handles most of the finances anyway, which is a blessing because I've never been much good with numbers. 

Though speaking of numbers, the school district just changed our grading software again. They switched us to this new cloud-based system over the summer, and it is just the most convoluted interface you could possibly imagine. I spent three hours on the phone with the IT help desk last Tuesday just trying to figure out how to input the mid-term grades. The poor boy on the phone sounded like he was about twelve years old, and he kept asking me to clear my cache. I told him I did that, but he insisted I do it again. I swear, they hire these kids right out of high school and expect them to know how to fix everything. My oldest daughter's first job was actually at a call center for a catalog company, selling those fleece-lined slippers... they were so popular back in the late nineties, remember those? She hated it, but it paid for her first car. A little blue Honda Civic that smelled faintly of wet dog, even though we never owned a dog...
Aside from the restlessness you've mentioned, have you been feeling persistently sad, down, or lacking interest and pleasure in the things you usually enjoy over these past eight months?

Sad? Oh, heavens no. I haven't been feeling sad or down at all. I mean, I still love teaching, and I still enjoy my book club, even if I do have trouble sitting still through the discussions sometimes. But no, no loss of interest or anything like that. 

Actually, speaking of book club, we're reading this fascinating biography of Eleanor Roosevelt right now. Did you know she used to write a daily newspaper column? Every single day! I can barely manage to write my weekly lesson plans without getting distracted by something else. Last week, I sat down to plan out our unit on the Roaring Twenties, and before I knew it, I was looking up vintage flapper dresses on the internet. They had such beautiful beadwork back then, didn't they? Real craftsmanship. You just don't see that kind of attention to detail in clothing anymore. Nowadays, everything is just mass-produced and falls apart after three washes. I bought a blouse from a department store just last month, wore it once, and a button popped right off while I was writing on the chalkboard. So embarrassing! I had to use a safety pin for the rest of the afternoon...
Looking back at your childhood, were you often described as restless, easily distracted, or 'bouncing off the walls' when you were in elementary school?

Oh, absolutely. Even when I was a little girl, my teachers always wrote on my report cards that I was a bright student but I just could not stay in my seat or wait my turn to speak. My mother used to joke that I had worn a literal path in the floorboards between my desk and the pencil sharpener before I even turned ten! 

Though, speaking of pencil sharpeners, you know they really don't make those sturdy metal crank ones anymore. The ones we had in my elementary school—Lincoln Elementary, over on 4th Street, though they tore it down in the eighties to build a strip mall, which was a real shame—anyway, those old wall-mounted sharpeners were practically indestructible. Now, in my classroom, the kids all have these cheap little plastic battery-operated things, or they just use mechanical pencils. I cannot stand mechanical pencils. The lead snaps if you press even a little bit too hard, and then you have those tiny little bits of graphite all over the desks. It gets right on the cuffs of my sleeves when I'm leaning over to help a student with their work. I buy these nice white blouses from Macy's, and getting graphite stains out of the cuffs is just a nightmare. You really have to pre-treat it with dish soap before you put it in the wash, otherwise the gray just sets right into the fabric...
